items.stem: What is skimming?
options: Reading quickly to get the overall gist of a text
Searching for one specific detail such as a date
Reading a text aloud to check fluency
Reading every word slowly to analyse language
items.answer: Reading quickly to get the overall gist of a text
items.markingKey: Skimming = fast reading for the general idea, using titles, headings and the first and last sentences of paragraphs.

items.stem: Explain the difference between skimming and scanning, giving an example of when you would use each in Paper 1.
items.answer: Skimming is reading quickly for the overall gist, e.g. a first read of the passage to see what it is about; scanning is searching for a particular detail, e.g. finding a time or number needed for a one-mark question.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: skimming = gist; 1 mark: scanning = specific detail; up to 1 further mark for appropriate exam examples. [3]

items.stem: Explain why it is useful to skim the whole passage before answering the first question.
items.answer: Skimming first gives an overview of the content, structure and text type, so you know where to look for answers and can understand details in context; it also prevents misreading the purpose.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: overview / knowing where information is; 1 mark: context helps interpret details or saves time later. [2]

items.stem: Scan this extract from the letter to a newspaper ‘Protect Our Night Sky’ to answer the questions. “As a member of the town’s astronomy club for over twenty years, I have watched our night sky disappear.” How long has the writer belonged to the astronomy club?
items.answer: Over twenty years.
items.markingKey: Over twenty years. [1]

items.stem: Use scanning to find the answers in this part of the short story ‘Stranded’. “Kenji and his sister had been walking since dawn, and the hut they were aiming for was still two hours away. … It came over the crest with a howl, snatching Aiko’s hat and flinging it into the valley before either of them could move. … ‘We go back,’ Aiko shouted, ‘to the overhang!’ He wanted to argue — they had come so far — but she was already turning, and he knew she was right.” (a) What did the wind take from Aiko? (b) How far away was the hut when the storm began? (c) Identify the type of text this extract comes from. (d) Name the key word or phrase you scanned for to answer the first question, and explain why it helped.
items.answer: (a) Her hat. (b) Two hours’ walk away. (c) Short story. (d) A key word from the question, e.g. ‘snatching Aiko’s hat’, which leads directly to the answer.
items.markingKey: (a) Her hat. [1] (b) Two hours’ walk away. [1] (c) short story [1] (d) any appropriate key word linked to the question; 1 mark for the explanation [2]

items.stem: Read the short story ‘Stranded’: “By three o’clock the sky over the ridge had turned the colour of a bruise. Kenji and his sister had been walking since dawn, and the hut they were aiming for was still two hours away. The first drops of rain were fat and slow, almost playful. Then the wind arrived. It came over the crest with a howl, snatching Aiko’s hat and flinging it into the valley before either of them could move. The path, which had been a friendly ribbon of gravel all morning, became a stream. Kenji’s boots filled with icy water. He could hear his own heartbeat louder than the thunder. ‘We go back,’ Aiko shouted, ‘to the overhang!’ He wanted to argue — they had come so far — but she was already turning, and he knew she was right. They stumbled downhill, clutching at roots and rocks, until the dark mouth of the overhang opened in front of them. Inside, it was dry and smelled of moss. They sat shoulder to shoulder, shaking, and listened to the mountain roar.” (a) Skim the text and state its gist in one sentence. (b) Where did Aiko decide they should go? (c) How far away was the hut when the storm began?
items.answer: (a) A brother and sister walking in the mountains are caught by a sudden storm and shelter under a rock overhang. (b) Back to the overhang, a rock shelter. (c) Two hours’ walk away.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: main topic or situation; 1 mark: outcome or main point – A brother and sister walking in the mountains are caught by a sudden storm and shelter under a rock overhang. [2] (b) Back to the overhang, a rock shelter. [1] (c) Two hours’ walk away. [1]

items.stem: You skim the speech ‘Speech to the Youth Climate Forum’. It begins: ‘Friends, I want to begin with a number: eleven.’ and ends: ‘That is exactly the point.’ Explain what the gist of the whole text is likely to be, and how these sentences helped you.
items.answer: A student explains how a school eco-club noticed lost trees, proved their cooling effect and planted saplings for the future. The opening sets up the situation/topic and the ending shows its outcome or main message.
items.markingKey: Mark points: 1 mark for a reasonable statement of the gist (A student explains how a school eco-club noticed lost trees, proved their cooling effect and planted saplings for the future.); further mark(s) for explaining how the opening and closing sentences signal topic, situation or conclusion.

items.stem: Which feature is most typical of a news article?
options: A list of instructions in the imperative
An opening sentence that summarises who, what, when and where
items.answer: An opening sentence that summarises who, what, when and where
items.markingKey: News articles open with the key facts.

items.stem: Read these lines from a leaflet: “Help us keep it that way by following these simple guidelines. Never stand on or touch the coral.” Identify the likely audience and purpose, and explain how one feature of the writing shows this.
items.answer: Audience: tourists visiting a marine park. Purpose: to give instructions and advice. Feature: short, clear sections of advice, which suits this audience and purpose.
items.markingKey: Mark points: 1 mark audience (tourists visiting a marine park); 1 mark purpose (to give instructions and advice); 1 mark for a relevant feature with brief explanation (e.g. short, clear sections of advice).

items.stem: Read these lines from a short story: “The silence she left behind was enormous. Tomás closed his eyes and pictured the kitchen at home, the grey light at six o’clock, his mother pretending to sleep through his scales.” Identify the likely audience and purpose, and explain how one feature of the writing shows this.
items.answer: Audience: general readers of fiction. Purpose: to entertain readers with a story. Feature: descriptive language and imagery to create mood, which suits this audience and purpose.
items.markingKey: Mark points: 1 mark audience (general readers of fiction); 1 mark purpose (to entertain readers with a story); 1 mark for a relevant feature with brief explanation (e.g. descriptive language and imagery to create mood).

items.stem: Read this extract from the opinion article ‘Should Homework Be Banned?’: “Beyond that, the benefits fall away and stress rises. Yet many teenagers report three or more hours a night, squeezed in between sport, chores and part-time jobs. I am not arguing for banning homework altogether.” Explain how the register (level of formality) suits the audience.
items.answer: The register suits parents and teachers reading a newspaper: direct and persuasive.
items.markingKey: identifies register; links to audience [2]

items.stem: Read this extract from the letter to a newspaper ‘Protect Our Night Sky’: “It disturbs the sleep of nearby residents, confuses migrating birds and wastes a great deal of public money. A simple solution exists: motion-sensor lighting, which switches on only when someone is present. Other towns have done it.” (a) Identify the text type. (b) Give two features typical of this text type, supporting one with a quotation from the extract.
items.answer: (a) Letter to a newspaper. (b) A polite but firm argument; ‘Dear Editor’ and a formal sign-off.
items.markingKey: (a) letter to a newspaper [1] (b) 1 mark per relevant feature; quotation must support the feature [2]

items.stem: Extract A is from the travel writing ‘Crossing the Salt Flats’: “Nothing prepares you for the whiteness. We left the last village at sunrise, and within twenty minutes the land had flattened into a blinding plain of salt that stretched to every horizon.” Extract B is from the news article ‘Flood Recovery in the River District’: “Three months after the River Kali burst its banks, recovery in the River District is uneven. Of the 1,400 homes flooded, around 900 have been repaired and reoccupied.” (a) Identify the text type and purpose of Extract A. (b) Identify the text type and purpose of Extract B.
items.answer: (a) Travel writing; to recount and reflect on a personal experience. (b) News article; to report news events.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark type; 1 mark purpose [2] (b) 1 mark type; 1 mark purpose [2]

items.stem: Read this extract from the travel writing ‘Crossing the Salt Flats’: “Nothing prepares you for the whiteness. We left the last village at sunrise, and within twenty minutes the land had flattened into a blinding plain of salt that stretched to every horizon. Our driver, Luis, wore two pairs of sunglasses at once and still squinted.” State the main purpose of the text.
items.answer: To recount and reflect on a personal experience.
items.markingKey: to recount and reflect on a personal experience [1]

items.stem: In ‘unpaid’, what does the prefix ‘un-’ mean?
items.answer: not
items.markingKey: ‘un-’ = not; unpaid = not paid.

items.stem: Explain two strategies you can use to work out the meaning of an unfamiliar word in a passage.
items.answer: Use context: read the words and sentences around it for synonyms, contrasts or examples; use word structure: break it into prefix, root and suffix (e.g. un-paid).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each for two distinct, explained strategies (context clues; word parts; substitution test; knowledge of related words). [2]

items.stem: Explain why you should test your guessed meaning by substituting it back into the sentence.
items.answer: If the substitute makes sense and keeps the meaning of the sentence, the guess is probably right; if not, the context shows you need a different meaning.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: substitution checks sense; 1 mark: reveals wrong guesses / multiple meanings. [2]

items.stem: Re-read these sentences from the travel writing ‘Crossing the Salt Flats’: “Our driver, Luis, wore two pairs of sunglasses at once and still squinted. … We had come in the dry season, so instead the ground was cracked into hexagons, each one rimmed with a crust of salt as neat as icing on a cake.” (a) Give the meaning of ‘rimmed’ as it is used in the text. (b) Identify the clue in the surrounding words that helps you understand ‘rimmed’.
items.answer: (a) Edged around the border. (b) Each hexagon has salt around its edge.
items.markingKey: (a) Edged around the border (accept close synonyms that fit the context) [1] (b) each hexagon has salt around its edge [1]

items.stem: Read this extract from the magazine article ‘The Return of the Urban Beekeeper’: “While farmland bees may feed on a single crop for weeks, city bees forage in parks, gardens, balconies and roadside verges, collecting nectar from hundreds of different plants. … Some ecologists warn that too many honeybee hives in a small area can leave too little food for wild bees, which are often more important pollinators.” (a) Give the meaning of ‘forage’ as it is used in the text. (b) Identify the clue in the surrounding words that helps you understand ‘forage’. (c) Identify the clue in the surrounding words that helps you understand ‘verges’.
items.answer: (a) Search widely for food. (b) Bees ‘forage’ in many places, ‘collecting nectar’. (c) They are ‘roadside’.
items.markingKey: (a) Search widely for food (accept close synonyms that fit the context) [1] (b) bees ‘forage’ in many places, ‘collecting nectar’ [1] (c) they are ‘roadside’ [1]

items.stem: In the short story ‘First Day at the Workshop’, a student meets two unfamiliar words: ‘The workshop smelled of pine resin and hot glue, and every surface was furred with sawdust.’ and ‘By the time I had finished, my arms ached and the floor gleamed, but he only grunted and handed me a piece of sandpaper and a scrap of rough timber.’ The student guesses that ‘furred’ means ‘freshly painted’ and ‘grunted’ means ‘sang quietly’. (a) Using the context, explain why the guess for ‘furred’ is wrong and give the correct meaning. (b) Using the context, explain why the guess for ‘grunted’ is wrong and give the correct meaning.
items.answer: (a) It means covered with a soft, thick layer; it describes surfaces covered ‘with sawdust’, so ‘freshly painted’ does not fit. (b) It means made a short, low sound instead of speaking; ‘but he only’ shows a minimal reaction rather than words of praise, so ‘sang quietly’ does not fit.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: correct meaning; 1 mark: explanation using context [2] (b) 1 mark: correct meaning; 1 mark: explanation using context [2]

items.stem: In the short story ‘The Last Mango Tree’, a student meets two unfamiliar words: ‘Most of the trees were already gone; the developers had cleared the eastern field in a single week, and now orange flags fluttered where the guavas had been.’ and ‘Most of the trees were already gone; the developers had cleared the eastern field in a single week, and now orange flags fluttered where the guavas had been.’ The student guesses that ‘developers’ means ‘farmers who grow fruit’ and ‘fluttered’ means ‘burned slowly’. (a) Using the context, explain why the guess for ‘developers’ is wrong and give the correct meaning. (b) Using the context, explain why the guess for ‘fluttered’ is wrong and give the correct meaning. (c) Explain why working out vocabulary in context matters for later questions on the passage.
items.answer: (a) It means people or companies who buy land in order to build on it; they ‘cleared’ the field and put up ‘orange flags’, which suggests construction, so ‘farmers who grow fruit’ does not fit. (b) It means moved lightly and quickly in the wind; flags are light and move in the breeze, so ‘burned slowly’ does not fit. (c) Misunderstanding a key word can lead to wrong inferences and weak analysis of the writer’s effects.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: correct meaning; 1 mark: explanation using context [2] (b) 1 mark: correct meaning; 1 mark: explanation using context [2] (c) link to inference or language questions [1]

items.stem: What is the main purpose of annotating a passage in the exam?
options: To count the words in the passage
To mark the material relevant to a specific question so it can be used efficiently
items.answer: To mark the material relevant to a specific question so it can be used efficiently
items.markingKey: Annotation is targeted at the task, not general highlighting.

items.stem: Explain why highlighting almost the whole passage is an ineffective way to annotate.
items.answer: If everything is highlighted, nothing stands out; you still have to reread to find the relevant points, wasting time and risking irrelevant material.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: loss of focus/nothing stands out; 1 mark: wastes time or leads to irrelevance. [2]

items.stem: Explain how numbering points in the margin helps when answering a question that asks for a set number of ideas.
items.answer: Numbering lets you check you have enough distinct points, avoid repeating the same idea and plan the order of your answer.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: counting/coverage; 1 mark: avoids repetition or helps ordering. [2]

items.stem: Annotate this extract from the autobiography ‘Learning to Swim at Forty’ for a task on the writer’s experience of the swimming lessons. List each relevant point in a short note of your own. “So when I signed up for beginners’ lessons at the age of forty, I expected to be laughed at. Instead, I found myself in the shallow end with a retired bus driver, two nurses and a nineteen-year-old student who was terrified of putting her face in the water. Our instructor, Hana, was half my age and endlessly patient. ‘Your body wants to float,’ she kept saying. ‘You just have to stop fighting it.’”
items.answer: Expected to be mocked as a forty-year-old beginner; Joined a mixed class of other nervous adults; Had a young, very patient instructor.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per relevant point (max 3): expected to be mocked as a forty-year-old beginner; joined a mixed class of other nervous adults; had a young, very patient instructor. No credit for copied irrelevant detail.

items.stem: Annotate this extract from the leaflet ‘Visiting the Coral Reef Responsibly’ for a task on how visitors can protect the reef and its wildlife. List each relevant point in a short note of your own. “Help us keep it that way by following these simple guidelines. Never stand on or touch the coral. It may look like rock, but it is a living animal, and a single touch can damage its delicate outer layer. Use reef-safe sun cream.”
items.answer: Do not touch or stand on coral; Use reef-safe sun cream.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per relevant point (max 2): do not touch or stand on coral; use reef-safe sun cream. No credit for copied irrelevant detail.

items.stem: Annotate this extract from the travel writing ‘Crossing the Salt Flats’ for a task on what makes the salt flats an unusual place to visit. List each relevant point in a short note of your own. Then group your points under two headings. “We left the last village at sunrise, and within twenty minutes the land had flattened into a blinding plain of salt that stretched to every horizon. Our driver, Luis, wore two pairs of sunglasses at once and still squinted. In the rainy season, he told us, a thin layer of water turns the flats into the world’s largest mirror, and the sky appears both above and below you. We had come in the dry season, so instead the ground was cracked into hexagons, each one rimmed with a crust of salt as neat as icing on a cake. At noon Luis stopped the jeep and switched off the engine.”
items.answer: A dazzling white plain stretches to every horizon; In the rainy season it reflects the sky like a vast mirror; In the dry season the ground forms salt-edged hexagons. Headings: appearance / atmosphere.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per relevant point (max 3): a dazzling white plain stretches to every horizon; in the rainy season it reflects the sky like a vast mirror; in the dry season the ground forms salt-edged hexagons. 1 mark for sensible grouping. No credit for copied irrelevant detail.

items.stem: Read the news article ‘Flood Recovery in the River District’: “Three months after the River Kali burst its banks, recovery in the River District is uneven. Of the 1,400 homes flooded, around 900 have been repaired and reoccupied. The remaining families are still living with relatives or in temporary housing at the sports centre. The main road bridge, which was closed after cracks were found in its supports, reopened last week following emergency repairs costing 2.3 million dollars. However, the district’s only secondary school remains shut, and around 600 students are being taught in shifts at a primary school four kilometres away. Local businesses have been hit hard. A survey by the traders’ association found that one in five shops has not reopened, and many owners say their insurance did not cover flood damage. Engineers have recommended raising the flood wall by one metre and restoring wetlands upstream to slow the water in future. The regional government says it will publish its decision by the end of the year.” (a) Sort the relevant details in the text under two headings: ‘progress’ and ‘problems’. (b) Explain why you would not annotate this sentence for the task: ‘The regional government says it will publish its decision by the end of the year.’
items.answer: (a) progress: about 900 homes repaired and lived in again, the main bridge has reopened; problems: hundreds of families still displaced, the secondary school is still closed, students taught in shifts far away, a fifth of shops still shut. (b) It does not give information about the progress made since the flood and the problems that remain; it adds background, description or an example rather than a key point.
items.markingKey: (a) accurate grouping [2] (b) 1 mark: not relevant to the focus; 1 mark: explains what kind of material it is [2]

items.stem: Read the speech ‘Speech to the Youth Climate Forum’: “Friends, I want to begin with a number: eleven. That is how many trees stood in our school playground when my mother was a pupil there. Today there is one. The others were cut down, one by one, for a car park, a new science block and a wider gate. Nobody meant any harm. Nobody stopped to count. And that, I believe, is how we lose most things — not in a single disaster, but in small decisions that nobody notices. Last year our eco-club decided to notice. We measured the playground at midday in June: 41 degrees on the tarmac, 29 in the shade of that one remaining tree. Twelve degrees. Think about that the next time someone tells you trees are decoration. So we raised money, we wrote to the council, and in November we planted twenty saplings. Some will die. Most will grow. In twenty years, a pupil you will never meet will sit in their shade and not even think about it. That is exactly the point.” (a) Sort the relevant details in the text under two headings: ‘actions’ and ‘reasons’. (b) Explain why you would not annotate this sentence for the task: ‘Friends, I want to begin with a number: eleven.’
items.answer: (a) actions: they paid attention to tree loss, they measured playground temperatures, raised money, contacted the council, planted twenty young trees; reasons: shade was twelve degrees cooler, to benefit future pupils. (b) It does not give information about what the eco-club did and why; it adds background, description or an example rather than a key point.
items.markingKey: (a) accurate grouping [2] (b) 1 mark: not relevant to the focus; 1 mark: explains what kind of material it is [2]

items.stem: Which annotation is most useful when preparing a summary on ‘the causes of waste’?
options: Underlining each separate cause and numbering it in the margin
items.answer: Underlining each separate cause and numbering it in the margin
items.markingKey: Numbering separate points helps avoid repetition and count content.

items.stem: What is scanning?
options: Reading the whole text closely for implied meanings
Searching a text quickly for a specific piece of information
Summarising a text in your own words
items.answer: Searching a text quickly for a specific piece of information
items.markingKey: Scanning = looking for particular details (names, numbers, key words) without reading everything.

items.stem: Explain why you should underline the key words in a question before scanning the passage.
items.answer: Key words tell you exactly what information is needed (e.g. a reason, a time, a feeling), so you scan for the right detail and do not copy irrelevant material.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: focuses the search; 1 mark: avoids irrelevant or wrong information. [2]

items.stem: Scan this extract from the autobiography ‘Learning to Swim at Forty’ to answer the questions. “For four weeks I fought it.” For how long did the writer struggle before managing to float?
items.answer: Four weeks.
items.markingKey: Four weeks. [1]

items.stem: Read the review ‘Review: The Floating Museum’: “Housed in a converted cargo ship moored in Lisbon’s harbour, the new Museum of the Sea promises ‘an unforgettable voyage through five centuries of ocean history’. For the most part, it delivers. The lower deck is the star attraction: a dimly lit gallery where a full-size whale skeleton hangs above visitors’ heads, slowly revolving as if still swimming. Children around me gasped; one small boy refused to leave. The interactive navigation room, where you can steer a virtual ship through a storm, is equally gripping, although the queue on the Saturday I visited lasted forty minutes. Less successful is the upper deck, which is crammed with glass cases of maps and instruments labelled in tiny print. After the drama below, it feels like reading a textbook in a cupboard. The café, meanwhile, is overpriced: eight euros for a sandwich and a juice. Overall, though, this is a bold, imaginative museum that deserves its crowds. Go early, go hungry for wonder — and bring your own lunch.” (a) Where is the museum housed? (b) How many centuries of history does the museum promise to cover? (c) Identify the type of text and give two features from the text that helped you identify it while skimming.
items.answer: (a) In a converted cargo ship moored in Lisbon’s harbour. (b) Five centuries. (c) Review: evaluation of strengths and weaknesses; first-person opinion.
items.markingKey: (a) In a converted cargo ship moored in Lisbon’s harbour. [1] (b) Five centuries. [1] (c) 1 mark: review; 1 mark each for two relevant features with reference to the text [3]

items.stem: “The main road bridge, which was closed after cracks were found in its supports, reopened last week following emergency repairs costing 2.3 million dollars. However, the district’s only secondary school remains shut, and around 600 students are being taught in shifts at a primary school four kilometres away.” From which type of text is this extract most likely taken?
items.answer: news article
items.markingKey: News article: e.g. an opening that summarises who, what, when and where; facts and figures.

items.stem: Read these lines from a memoir: “It was only after she died, when I found her handwritten notebook hidden behind the rice tin, that I understood. There were no quantities in it at all — just names.” Identify the likely audience and purpose, and explain how one feature of the writing shows this.
items.answer: Audience: adult readers of a collection of family memories. Purpose: to recount and reflect on a personal experience. Feature: quoted speech of remembered people, which suits this audience and purpose.
items.markingKey: Mark points: 1 mark audience (adult readers of a collection of family memories); 1 mark purpose (to recount and reflect on a personal experience); 1 mark for a relevant feature with brief explanation (e.g. quoted speech of remembered people).

items.stem: Read this extract from the report ‘Canteen Food Waste Report’: “Purpose: This report presents the findings of a two-week survey of food waste in the school canteen and recommends ways to reduce it. Findings: Students threw away an average of 41 kilograms of food each day. The largest single source of waste was rice, which accounted for almost a third of the total, followed by cooked vegetables.” Give two features typical of this text type, supporting one with a quotation from the extract.
items.answer: Statistics and findings; numbered or sequenced recommendations.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per relevant feature; quotation must support the feature [2]

items.stem: A reader does not know the word ‘unpaid’. Using the surrounding words in ‘Like the rest of the team, he is an unpaid volunteer; by day he teaches mathematics at a local secondary school.’ (from the interview ‘The Mountain Rescue Volunteer’), explain how they could work out what it means.
items.answer: ‘unpaid’ means not receiving money for work. Context clue: he has a separate job ‘by day’.
items.markingKey: Mark points: 1 mark for an accurate meaning (not receiving money for work); 1 mark for identifying the clue in the context (he has a separate job ‘by day’).

items.stem: Here is part of the short story ‘The Last Mango Tree’: “Most of the trees were already gone; the developers had cleared the eastern field in a single week, and now orange flags fluttered where the guavas had been.” (a) Identify the clue in the surrounding words that helps you understand ‘developers’. (b) Give the meaning of ‘fluttered’ as it is used in the text.
items.answer: (a) They ‘cleared’ the field and put up ‘orange flags’, which suggests construction. (b) Moved lightly and quickly in the wind.
items.markingKey: (a) they ‘cleared’ the field and put up ‘orange flags’, which suggests construction [1] (b) Moved lightly and quickly in the wind (accept close synonyms that fit the context) [1]

items.stem: Here is part of the memoir ‘My Grandmother’s Kitchen’: “For years my attempts were either bland or so fiery that my friends wept.” (a) Give the meaning of ‘bland’ as it is used in the text. (b) Identify the clue in the surrounding words that helps you understand ‘bland’. (c) Identify the clue in the surrounding words that helps you understand ‘fiery’.
items.answer: (a) Without much flavour. (b) It is the opposite of ‘so fiery’. (c) It made ‘my friends wept’, so it was painfully hot.
items.markingKey: (a) Without much flavour (accept close synonyms that fit the context) [1] (b) it is the opposite of ‘so fiery’ [1] (c) it made ‘my friends wept’, so it was painfully hot [1]

items.stem: A student underlines ‘Every evening she climbed the 117 iron steps of the tower, wound the clockwork that turned the great lens, and wrote the weather in a leather logbook in her small, upright handwriting.’ in the biography ‘The Lighthouse Keeper’s Last Winter’ when preparing to write about Elena’s duties as keeper and how her working life ended. Explain why this is a good choice and suggest a short margin label.
items.answer: It is relevant because it shows that climbed the tower every evening. Margin note: “climbed the tower every evening”.
items.markingKey: Mark points: 1 mark: links the sentence to the focus (Elena’s duties as keeper and how her working life ended); 1 mark: concise own-words note, e.g. “climbed the tower every evening”.

items.stem: Explain why you should annotate with the question’s focus in mind rather than simply marking interesting language.
items.answer: Different questions need different material; interesting language may be irrelevant to, say, a summary of causes, so annotation must serve the task.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: task determines relevance; 1 mark: example of irrelevant but interesting material. [2]

items.stem: Annotate this extract from the opinion article ‘Should Homework Be Banned?’ for a task on the writer’s arguments against too much homework and the changes proposed. List each relevant point in a short note of your own. “Research suggests that for primary pupils homework makes little difference to achievement, while for older students modest amounts — around an hour a night — can help. Beyond that, the benefits fall away and stress rises. Yet many teenagers report three or more hours a night, squeezed in between sport, chores and part-time jobs. I am not arguing for banning homework altogether. Reading for pleasure, practising a musical instrument or revising for a test are valuable habits.”
items.answer: It barely helps younger pupils; Beyond an hour it adds stress without benefit; Teenagers have far too much.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per relevant point (max 3): it barely helps younger pupils; beyond an hour it adds stress without benefit; teenagers have far too much. No credit for copied irrelevant detail.

items.stem: Read the interview ‘The Mountain Rescue Volunteer’: “Sipho Ndlovu has been called out 212 times in eleven years with the Drakensberg mountain rescue team, and he still keeps his boots by the front door. ‘The phone can ring at three in the morning,’ he says. ‘You have perhaps ten minutes to be in the truck.’ Like the rest of the team, he is an unpaid volunteer; by day he teaches mathematics at a local secondary school. Most call-outs, he explains, are not dramatic falls but simple mistakes: hikers who set off too late, who underestimate how quickly the weather changes, or who rely on a phone battery that dies on the mountain. The worst night he remembers was a search for two teenagers in thick cloud. ‘We found them at dawn, cold and frightened but alive. I have never been so tired or so happy.’ Asked why he continues, he shrugs. ‘Someone came for my father once, years ago. I suppose I am paying it back.’” (a) Sort the relevant details in the text under two headings: ‘hikers’ mistakes’ and ‘what volunteering involves’. (b) Explain why you would not annotate this sentence for the task: ‘Asked why he continues, he shrugs.’
items.answer: (a) hikers’ mistakes: hikers start too late, they underestimate sudden weather changes, they rely on phones whose batteries fail; what volunteering involves: volunteers are called at any hour, they must be ready within minutes, they are unpaid and have other jobs. (b) It does not give information about the common mistakes that lead to rescues and what volunteering involves; it adds background, description or an example rather than a key point.
items.markingKey: (a) accurate grouping [2] (b) 1 mark: not relevant to the focus; 1 mark: explains what kind of material it is [2]

items.stem: Read the blog ‘Street Food Fridays’: “Every Friday at six, the car park behind Colombo’s old railway station turns into the best restaurant in the city. No tables, no menus, no reservations — just thirty-odd stalls, a few strings of coloured bulbs and a crowd that grows until you can barely move. My first stop is always Ravi’s kottu stall, where two flat-topped grills clatter like a drum band as he chops roti, egg and vegetables together with a pair of steel blades. A plate costs less than a bus ticket. Next, I queue for hoppers: crisp, bowl-shaped pancakes with a soft egg at the centre. I have burned my fingers on them every single week and I regret nothing. Not everything is perfect. There are not enough bins, and by nine the ground is littered with paper plates. But the council has promised more bins from next month, and the traders now run a tidy-up rota. Come hungry, bring cash, and wear shoes you don’t mind ruining.” (a) Select 4 separate details relevant to what makes Street Food Fridays appealing and the problems it faces, writing each as a short note. (b) Sort the relevant details in the text under two headings: ‘appeal’ and ‘problems’.
items.answer: (a) A lively, colourful atmosphere; Cooking is a lively performance; Food is very cheap; Delicious local dishes such as hoppers; It becomes extremely crowded; There are too few bins, so litter builds up. (b) appeal: a lively, colourful atmosphere, cooking is a lively performance, food is very cheap, delicious local dishes such as hoppers; problems: it becomes extremely crowded, there are too few bins, so litter builds up.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per relevant, distinct point up to 4 [4] (b) accurate grouping [2]

items.stem: Which parts of a non-fiction text are most useful when skimming for gist?
options: Only the last word of each paragraph
The title, subheadings and the first sentence of each paragraph
items.answer: The title, subheadings and the first sentence of each paragraph
items.markingKey: Headings and topic sentences carry the main ideas.

items.stem: Explain why scanning alone is not enough to answer a question beginning ‘What does this suggest about…?’
items.answer: Scanning finds where the relevant words are, but ‘suggest’ asks for an inference; you must read the surrounding text closely and interpret what is implied.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: scanning only locates; 1 mark: inference needs close reading of implied meaning. [2]

items.stem: Scan the following lines from the short story ‘The Power Cut’. “When the power returned at 9.02, flooding the room with harsh white light, I was almost disappointed.” When did the power return?

Read the short story ‘The Power Cut’: “The lights died at 7.14, halfway through dinner. For a moment nobody moved. Then my little sister laughed, a high nervous sound, and Dad’s chair scraped back as he went to find the torch he swore was in the drawer by the sink. It was not. Outside, the whole street had vanished; even the streetlamps were blind. I had never seen our neighbourhood so dark. Without the hum of the fridge and the murmur of the television, the house seemed to hold its breath. We found three candles in the end, stubby and half-melted from someone’s birthday cake, and set them in a saucer in the middle of the table. In their wobbling light my parents’ faces looked younger, softer. Mum told a story about a storm in her village when she was a girl, a story I had never heard before. Nobody reached for a phone. When the power returned at 9.02, flooding the room with harsh white light, I was almost disappointed.” (a) Skim the text and state its gist in one sentence. (b) Explain why you would need to read closely, rather than scan, to answer this question, and then answer it: What does this suggest about the narrator’s feelings about the power cut?
items.answer: (a) During an evening power cut a family gathers by candlelight and rediscovers each other. (b) It asks for an inference, not a stated fact. The narrator enjoyed the closeness and calm it brought and was sorry to see it end.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: main topic or situation; 1 mark: outcome or main point – During an evening power cut a family gathers by candlelight and rediscovers each other. [2] (b) 1 mark: recognises it requires inference/implied meaning; 1 mark: the narrator enjoyed the closeness and calm it brought and was sorry to see it end. 1 mark: evidence, e.g. ‘I was almost disappointed’ [3]

items.stem: These lines come from a short story: “They stumbled downhill, clutching at roots and rocks, until the dark mouth of the overhang opened in front of them. Inside, it was dry and smelled of moss.” What is the main purpose of the text?
options: to present findings and make recommendations
to entertain readers with a story
to inform readers about a person
items.answer: to entertain readers with a story
items.markingKey: To entertain readers with a story: typical of a short story for general readers of fiction.

items.stem: “The café, meanwhile, is overpriced: eight euros for a sandwich and a juice. Overall, though, this is a bold, imaginative museum that deserves its crowds.” These lines are from a review. Explain who the text is written for and why, referring to one feature of its style.
items.answer: Audience: readers of a city culture guide. Purpose: to evaluate and recommend. Feature: an overall verdict and recommendation, which suits this audience and purpose.
items.markingKey: Mark points: 1 mark audience (readers of a city culture guide); 1 mark purpose (to evaluate and recommend); 1 mark for a relevant feature with brief explanation (e.g. an overall verdict and recommendation).

items.stem: Read this extract from the short story ‘First Day at the Workshop’: “I was not late; I was ten minutes early. I said nothing. He pointed his chin at a broom propped in the corner, and I understood that this was my first lesson.” Give two features typical of this text type, supporting one with a quotation from the extract.
items.answer: Descriptive language and imagery to create mood; third- or first-person narration of events.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per relevant feature; quotation must support the feature [2]

items.stem: A reader does not know the word ‘fixtures’. Using the surrounding words in ‘Waste was highest on Fridays, when a quarter of students said they skipped lunch to leave early for sports fixtures.’ (from the report ‘Canteen Food Waste Report’), explain how they could work out what it means.
items.answer: ‘fixtures’ means arranged sports matches or events. Context clue: students ‘leave early for sports fixtures’.
items.markingKey: Mark points: 1 mark for an accurate meaning (arranged sports matches or events); 1 mark for identifying the clue in the context (students ‘leave early for sports fixtures’).

items.stem: The following lines are taken from the biography ‘The Lighthouse Keeper’s Last Winter’: “In 1998 the lighthouse was automated, and a machine in a grey metal box took over her duties. … Most days she recorded only wind direction and visibility, but on her last night she wrote a single extra line: ‘Light shown. All ships safe. Keeper going home.’” (a) Give the meaning of ‘automated’ as it is used in the text. (b) Give the meaning of ‘visibility’ as it is used in the text.
items.answer: (a) Operated by machines rather than people. (b) How far you can see, depending on the weather.
items.markingKey: (a) Operated by machines rather than people (accept close synonyms that fit the context) [1] (b) How far you can see, depending on the weather (accept close synonyms that fit the context) [1]

items.stem: Re-read these sentences from the short story ‘The Audition’: “But now his fingers felt like they belonged to somebody else — stiff, cold, clumsy. … A man with a clipboard read out a name that was not his, and the cellist rose and glided away.” (a) Give the meaning of ‘glided’ as it is used in the text. (b) Give the meaning of ‘clumsy’ as it is used in the text. (c) Identify the clue in the surrounding words that helps you understand ‘clumsy’.
items.answer: (a) Moved smoothly and gracefully. (b) Awkward and badly controlled. (c) It is listed with ‘stiff’ and ‘cold’, which all describe fingers that will not work properly.
items.markingKey: (a) Moved smoothly and gracefully (accept close synonyms that fit the context) [1] (b) Awkward and badly controlled (accept close synonyms that fit the context) [1] (c) it is listed with ‘stiff’ and ‘cold’, which all describe fingers that will not work properly [1]

items.stem: A student underlines ‘We rescued thirty-two and reburied them in the hatchery enclosure, which took nearly two hours.’ in the diary ‘Turtle Hatchery Diary’ when preparing to write about the tasks the volunteers carry out. Explain why this is a good choice and suggest a short margin label.
items.answer: It is relevant because it shows that rescue damaged nests and rebury eggs in the enclosure. Margin note: “rescue damaged nests and rebury eggs in the enclosure”.
items.markingKey: Mark points: 1 mark: links the sentence to the focus (the tasks the volunteers carry out); 1 mark: concise own-words note, e.g. “rescue damaged nests and rebury eggs in the enclosure”.

items.stem: Explain why this sentence from the travel writing ‘Crossing the Salt Flats’ should be annotated for a task on what makes the salt flats an unusual place to visit, and write a brief margin note for it: ‘We had come in the dry season, so instead the ground was cracked into hexagons, each one rimmed with a crust of salt as neat as icing on a cake.’
items.answer: It is relevant because it shows that in the dry season the ground forms salt-edged hexagons. Margin note: “in the dry season the ground forms salt-edged hexagons”.
items.markingKey: Mark points: 1 mark: links the sentence to the focus (what makes the salt flats an unusual place to visit); 1 mark: concise own-words note, e.g. “in the dry season the ground forms salt-edged hexagons”.

items.stem: Annotate this extract from the travel writing ‘The Bus to Kathmandu’ for a task on the difficulties of the journey and the moments that made it bearable. List each relevant point in a short note of your own. “The road climbed in hairpin bends, and on the outside of each bend there was nothing at all — no barrier, no verge, only a sheer drop to a river that glittered like a thread of tin far below. I gripped the seat in front so hard my knuckles turned white. The woman beside me noticed. Without a word, she broke a piece from her bread and pressed it into my hand, then pointed out of the window at a line of snow peaks that had appeared above the clouds. For a moment I forgot to be afraid.”
items.answer: The road ran along terrifying unprotected drops; A stranger shared her bread; Beautiful mountain views.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per relevant point (max 3): the road ran along terrifying unprotected drops; a stranger shared her bread; beautiful mountain views. No credit for copied irrelevant detail.

items.stem: Read the autobiography ‘Learning to Swim at Forty’: “I grew up three streets from the sea and never learned to swim. As a child I told everyone I preferred sandcastles; as a teenager I said swimming was boring; as an adult I simply stopped going to the beach. So when I signed up for beginners’ lessons at the age of forty, I expected to be laughed at. Instead, I found myself in the shallow end with a retired bus driver, two nurses and a nineteen-year-old student who was terrified of putting her face in the water. Our instructor, Hana, was half my age and endlessly patient. ‘Your body wants to float,’ she kept saying. ‘You just have to stop fighting it.’ For four weeks I fought it. I sank like a dropped spanner. Then, one wet Tuesday in March, I lay back, spread my arms and felt the water lift me as gently as a hand under a sleeping child. I stayed there, staring at the steamed-up ceiling, and laughed out loud. Nobody laughed at me. They clapped.” (a) Sort the relevant details in the text under two headings: ‘how the writer felt’ and ‘what happened’. (b) Explain why you would not annotate this sentence for the task: ‘I grew up three streets from the sea and never learned to swim.’
items.answer: (a) how the writer felt: expected to be mocked as a forty-year-old beginner, felt joy and was applauded, not mocked; what happened: joined a mixed class of other nervous adults, had a young, very patient instructor, struggled and sank for a month, finally floated one day in March. (b) It does not give information about the writer’s experience of the swimming lessons; it adds background, description or an example rather than a key point.
items.markingKey: (a) accurate grouping [2] (b) 1 mark: not relevant to the focus; 1 mark: explains what kind of material it is [2]

items.stem: Read the biography ‘The Lighthouse Keeper’s Last Winter’: “For thirty-one years, Elena Petrova kept the light at Cape Morrow burning. Every evening she climbed the 117 iron steps of the tower, wound the clockwork that turned the great lens, and wrote the weather in a leather logbook in her small, upright handwriting. In 1998 the lighthouse was automated, and a machine in a grey metal box took over her duties. She was given a clock, a certificate and three weeks to leave. Her final logbook entry survives. Most days she recorded only wind direction and visibility, but on her last night she wrote a single extra line: ‘Light shown. All ships safe. Keeper going home.’ Villagers remember her walking down the cliff path the next morning without looking back, her suitcase in one hand and a geranium in a pot in the other. She lived another nineteen years in a flat overlooking the harbour. Neighbours said she still woke at dusk, every evening, and stood at the window until she saw the beam.” (a) Select 4 separate details relevant to Elena’s duties as keeper and how her working life ended, writing each as a short note. (b) Sort the relevant details in the text under two headings: ‘duties’ and ‘how it ended’.
items.answer: (a) Climbed the tower every evening; Wound the clockwork that turned the lens; Recorded the weather in a logbook; The lighthouse was automated in 1998; She received a clock and certificate; She had only three weeks to leave. (b) duties: climbed the tower every evening, wound the clockwork that turned the lens, recorded the weather in a logbook; how it ended: the lighthouse was automated in 1998, she received a clock and certificate, she had only three weeks to leave.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per relevant, distinct point up to 4 [4] (b) accurate grouping [2]
